idiom_name: java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantReadWriteLock on the JVM; kotlinx.coroutines has only an exclusive Mutex
implementation_notes: On the JVM Kotlin uses the JDK primitive unchanged - ReentrantReadWriteLock (or StampedLock) with readLock()/writeLock() in try/finally - because Kotlin's own concurrency surface is synchronized/@Synchronized (exclusive) and, for coroutines, a non-reentrant exclusive Mutex with withLock. There is no reader-writer lock in the Kotlin stdlib and none in kotlinx.coroutines: coroutine code either keeps read-mostly state in an immutable snapshot published through an atomic reference or StateFlow, or tolerates the exclusive Mutex. The classic form is still justified on the JVM for a thread-based component guarding a read-mostly cache; inside coroutines it must not be used, because a blocking lock occupies the dispatcher thread.
pitfalls: kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Mutex is exclusive and non-reentrant - there is no read/write variant, so model read-mostly state as immutable snapshots instead.
Blocking on a ReentrantReadWriteLock inside a coroutine starves (and can pin) the dispatcher; use withContext(Dispatchers.IO) or an exclusive Mutex in coroutine code.
synchronized/@Synchronized and read locks do not compose: mixing JVM monitor blocks with read/write locks invites lock-order deadlocks.
Read locks must be released in finally and never upgraded in place; the JVM attempt deadlocks exactly as the javadoc warns.
